title: The Measurement Problem
description: Why linear quantum dynamics clashes with definite outcomes, what decoherence fixes, and Wigner's friend

concepts.title: Bell's Dilemma: Not Everything, or Not Right
concepts.contentHtml:
The textbook recipe you met in Quantum Mechanics uses two different laws. Between measurements a quantum state evolves smoothly and deterministically under the Schrödinger equation; at a measurement it collapses at random to one outcome, with probabilities from the Born rule. Philosophy of physics begins by asking what this recipe claims about the world, and the first thing it notices is that the recipe never says exactly which processes count as measurements.

Run the argument yourself. A good detector reads "0" when a system is in state \(|0\rangle\) and "1" when it is in \(|1\rangle\). The Schrödinger equation is linear: feed it a sum of inputs and it returns the same sum of outputs. So if the system starts in a superposition \(a|0\rangle + b|1\rangle\) and you treat the detector as a quantum system too, the result is an entangled state in which the pointer reading is correlated with the system but has no definite value.1 If quantum theory is universal, it applies to the detector, to you and to the laboratory, and the dynamics alone never delivers a single reading.

John Bell put the choice bluntly: "Either the wavefunction, as given by the Schrödinger equation, is not everything, or it is not right.2" That sentence sorts every approach into three families:

  • The state is not everything. Either add something to it, as hidden-variable theories such as Bohmian mechanics do, or deny that it represents reality at all, as Copenhagen-style and QBist views do.3
  • The equation is not right. Modify the dynamics so that collapse becomes a real physical process, as GRW and other collapse theories do.
  • Neither horn. Keep the state complete and its evolution always unitary, and accept that every outcome happens, as Everett's many-worlds view does.

Every interpretation in this topic grasps one of these options, and each pays for it somewhere else.

concepts.title: Decoherence: What It Explains and What It Doesn't
concepts.contentHtml:
Real detectors are never isolated. Air molecules, photons and stray dust bounce off them constantly, and every collision carries away a trace of where the pointer is. Suppression of interference by such processes, decoherence, appears in papers from the early days of quantum mechanics, but the modern foundation of the subject was laid by H.-D. Zeh in the early 1970s,1 and W. Zurek's papers of the early 1980s were equally influential. Decoherence entangles a system with its environment so thoroughly that the different terms of a superposition can no longer interfere in any experiment you could realistically perform.

It is astonishingly fast. For a speck of dust a ten-thousandth of a millimetre in radius floating in air, interference between positions just \(10^{-13}\) cm apart is suppressed, and it reaches this after about a microsecond of exposure to air.2 That is why you never catch a dust grain, let alone a cat, in two places at once.

Does decoherence therefore solve the measurement problem? It is often said to, but physicists and philosophers alike have pointed out that it does not. Decoherence explains why you never observe superpositions of measurement results; it does not explain why you observe results at all.3 After decoherence the joint state of system, detector and environment is still a superposition, only now spread over more of the world. Including the environment actually widens the problem: the question is no longer just why pointers have readings, but why the whole classical world looks definite.

So decoherence is interpretation-neutral machinery. It matters to Everettian, Bohmian and collapse approaches alike, though it plays a different role in each, and it helped drive the extraordinary renaissance of Everett's theory in philosophy of physics since the mid-1990s,4 which you will meet in lesson 4.

concepts.title: Wigner's Friend: Whose Collapse Is It?
concepts.contentHtml:
The textbook recipe divides the world into a quantum system and an observer who is not described by the theory. Both John von Neumann and Werner Heisenberg emphasised that where you place this cut is somewhat arbitrary:1 put it between electron and detector, or between detector and the light reaching your retina, and the predictions come out the same. That freedom is harmless while there is one observer. In 1961 Eugene Wigner asked what happens when there are two.

Wigner imagined a friend who conducts an observation inside a sealed laboratory, while he himself treats the joint system of friend and experiment as a quantum system.2 For the friend there is a definite result. For Wigner, applying unitary quantum mechanics from outside, the whole lab is in an entangled superposition. Wigner concluded that conscious observers cannot be in superposition, so consciousness must trigger a physical collapse, involving "a violation of physical laws where consciousness plays a role". Few follow him that far today, but his scenario has become a precision tool.

In 2018 Daniela Frauchiger and Renato Renner introduced extended scenarios with more than two observers,3 each reasoning correctly with quantum theory about the others, and derived a contradiction. Their title states the moral they drew: "Quantum theory cannot consistently describe the use of itself". In 2020 Kok-Wei Bong, Howard Wiseman and colleagues proved that if quantum evolution is controllable on the scale of an observer, then one of No-Superdeterminism, Locality or Absoluteness of Observed Events (every observed event exists absolutely, not relatively) must be false.4 They tested their new inequality in a proof-of-principle experiment where a photon's path was deemed an observer.5 A 2019 six-photon experiment by Massimiliano Proietti and colleagues had violated a related inequality by 5 standard deviations.6

Read these results carefully. They are no-go theorems against combinations of assumptions, not refutations of any existing interpretation; each major approach can still describe the scenarios. What they force is a declaration. Bohmians keep absolute events and give up locality; Everettians, relationalists and QBists give up absoluteness; superdeterminists give up the freedom assumption.

title: Bell's Theorem and Nonlocality
description: EPR, Bell's inequality, the experiments that closed its loopholes, and what the 2022 Nobel settled

concepts.title: From EPR to the CHSH Inequality
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1935 Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen (EPR) argued that the quantum state cannot be a complete description of physical reality.1 Their example used entangled pairs: measure one particle and you can predict with certainty what a measurement on its distant partner will show. Unless measuring here instantly disturbs things there, they reasoned, the partner must have carried that answer all along, and quantum mechanics, which does not record it, is leaving something out.

For nearly three decades this looked like a matter of philosophical taste. Then in 1964 John Bell, a native of Northern Ireland working at CERN, published a paper in the short-lived journal Physics that turned it into an experimental question.2 Bell showed that if each particle carries its own instructions and no influence passes between the distant measurements, the correlations must obey an inequality, and that quantum mechanics predicts violations of it. His conclusion was stark: any hidden-variable theory that reproduces quantum statistics needs "a mechanism whereby the setting of one measuring device can influence the reading of another instrument, however remote3".

The version tested in laboratories is the CHSH inequality, derived by Clauser, Horne, Shimony and Holt in 1969. Alice chooses one of two settings, Bob one of two, and four correlations are combined into a single number \(S\). Every local hidden-variable theory obeys \(|S| \le 2\). Quantum mechanics reaches \(2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.83\), and Tsirelson showed in 1980 that this is the maximum violation of the CHSH inequality for any quantum state.4

Notice what does not prove anything. Perfect correlation when Alice and Bob choose the same setting, the case popular accounts love, can be reproduced by entirely local means, as Bell himself demonstrated with simple toy models.5 The force of the theorem lies in the pattern across mismatched settings.

concepts.title: Closing the Loopholes
concepts.contentHtml:
John Clauser took Bell's idea into the laboratory, using calcium atoms that emit entangled photons after being illuminated with a special light.1 In 1972 Freedman and Clauser found a result 6.5 standard deviations from the limit allowed by the CHSH inequality, in good agreement with quantum mechanics.2 Progress was not tidy: in 1973 a similar experiment by Holt and Pipkin, using mercury, came out in fairly good agreement with the inequality instead. Later experiments sided with quantum mechanics, but each left loopholes, extra assumptions a determined local realist could exploit:

  • Locality. If settings are fixed early, a signal could warn one side what the other will measure. In 1982 Aspect, Dalibard and Roger switched analyser orientations so rapidly that the choices were spacelike separated.3
  • Detection. If detectors miss many particles, the detected subset might be unrepresentative, so tests leaned on a fair-sampling assumption.
  • Freedom of choice. The settings might be correlated with the hidden variables at the source.

In 2015 three groups closed the locality and detection loopholes in a single experiment each. Hensen, Hanson and colleagues entangled electron spins 1.3 km apart4 and, over 245 trials, found \(S = 2.42 \pm 0.20\); the probability of a local-realist model producing a violation at least that large was only 0.039. Two photon experiments, led by Marissa Giustina and by Lynden Shalm, followed with far higher statistical significance, the first corresponding to an 11.5 standard deviation effect.5

Freedom of choice is harder, because any physical random-number generator might itself be correlated with the source. The BIG Bell Test used people instead. On 30 November 2016 about 100,000 participants playing an online video game generated 97,347,490 binary choices, which set the measurements in 13 experiments at 12 laboratories on five continents.6 Other tests have taken their settings from light emitted by Milky Way stars (2017) and by distant quasars (2018).

concepts.title: What Bell Rules Out: The 2022 Nobel and Its Fine Print
concepts.contentHtml:
On 4 October 2022 the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics to Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger1 "for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science". Zeilinger's group had gone on to demonstrate quantum teleportation,2 and the committee stressed the technology that grew from these tests: quantum computers, quantum networks and secure encrypted communication.

The press release summarised the physics by saying that quantum mechanics "cannot be replaced by a theory that uses hidden variables".3 Philosophers of physics wince at that sentence. Bell's theorem and the experiments rule out local hidden variables, or more exactly theories obeying Bell's local causality together with some auxiliary assumptions. Bohmian mechanics is a hidden-variable theory, and it survives because it is openly nonlocal. Jon Jarrett showed that Bell's locality condition is the conjunction of two parts:4 parameter independence (the result here does not depend on the distant setting) and outcome independence (it does not depend on the distant result). Bohmian mechanics violates parameter independence, yet it does not permit faster-than-light signalling.5

So the honest summary is a menu, and each camp chooses differently:

  • Reject local causality: Bohmian mechanics, and collapse theories such as GRW.
  • Reject unique outcomes: Everettian many worlds, where locality conditions must first be reformulated because every result occurs.
  • Reject measurement independence: superdeterminism, which supposes a common cause in the past that determines both settings and outcomes,6 or retrocausality, which lets causes act backwards in time.
  • Deny that the premises describe physical events: QBists, who hold that agents can use quantum theory with no appeal to non-local physical influences.

Bell did not tell us which option nature takes. He told us that there is no free lunch.

title: Copenhagen, QBism and Relational Views
description: Views that deny the quantum state is an observer-independent picture of reality, and what that costs

concepts.title: There Was No Single Copenhagen
concepts.contentHtml:
The view textbooks call "the Copenhagen interpretation" is less a doctrine than a family resemblance. The historian Don Howard argued in 2004 that "until Heisenberg coined the term in 1955, there was no unitary Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics.1" Niels Bohr's own view, complementarity, which he presented at Como in 1927,2 differs significantly from the textbook package of wave-particle duality and observer-induced collapse. Howard argues that it was Heisenberg's exposition, with its privileged role for the observer, that became identified with the Copenhagen name.

Bohr's central demand was that experiments be described in classical concepts: position, time, momentum and energy. The reason was not that apparatus obeys classical physics; Bohr did not think measuring devices always have to be described by classical dynamical laws. Rather, he held that these concepts are what physicists need for unambiguous communication about what happens in the laboratory.3 Quantum theory restricts their use. They cannot all be applied at once, so the whole experimental arrangement becomes part of what defines a phenomenon. On this view, properties like position and momentum can be attributed to an atomic object only in relation to a specific experimental arrangement.

Is this anti-realism? Scholars still disagree, and have read Bohr as an instrumentalist, an objective anti-realist, a phenomenological realist and a realist of various sorts.4 What realist critics object to is the shared cost: Copenhagen-style views give a reliable recipe for predictions but decline to say what physically happens during a measurement, which is exactly what the measurement problem asks. Defenders turn the point around. Bohr's firmness about classical concepts can be read as his response to the measurement problem, a claim that the demand for a story beneath the phenomena is itself the mistake.

concepts.title: QBism: The Quantum State Is Your Bet
concepts.contentHtml:
QBism, first called quantum Bayesianism, began as a collaboration between Carlton Caves, Christopher Fuchs and Rüdiger Schack at the turn of the 21st century, though Caves no longer considers himself a QBist;1 Fuchs, N. David Mermin and Schack later adopted the current name. Its central claim is radical. A quantum state does not represent a physical system at all. It represents the epistemic state of the agent who assigns it, concerning that agent's possible future experiences.2 Two physicists can legitimately assign different states to the same system, just as two punters can offer different odds on the same race.

The paradoxes then dissolve, QBists say. Collapse is not a physical event, merely the agent updating her credences in the light of experience. The Born rule becomes a normative requirement: an empirically motivated addition to the coherence conditions that keep a rational agent from accepting a Dutch book,3 a set of bets she is guaranteed to lose, come what may. Nonlocality goes too. Being present at a single location, an agent never experiences spatially separated events, so QBists argue that Bell correlations need no non-local physical influences. Fuchs, Mermin and Schack claim the view "removes the paradoxes, conundra, and pseudo-problems that have plagued quantum foundations for the past nine decades4".

The costs are as clear as the gains. The commonest objection is solipsism: if every state is personal, what is the shared world physics describes? Mermin replies that his belief that you are a being much like himself, with your own private experience, is "as firm a belief as any I have5". Harvey Brown complains that QBism's account of stimulation and response between agent and world "is not grounded in known physics", and Guido Bacciagaluppi has challenged the claim that the Born rule is a pure coherence condition. QBists answer that agents, actions and experiences are primitive terms that neither require nor admit a precise physical specification, and they count that as candour rather than evasion.

concepts.title: Relational Quantum Mechanics: Facts Between Systems
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1996 Carlo Rovelli proposed another way to give up observer-independence, with quantum gravity as a remote motivation.1 His model was relativity. Before Einstein, physicists were uneasy about the Lorentz transformations because they assumed time was the same for every observer; drop that assumption and the unease goes. Rovelli suggested the measurement problem comes from a similar incorrect notion: the notion of an observer-independent state of a system.2 In relational quantum mechanics (RQM), "different observers can give different accounts of the same set of events".

RQM differs from Copenhagen and QBism in a crucial way: there are no privileged observers and no appeal to minds or agents. Any physical system can play the role that Copenhagen gave to the observer.3 Variables take values only in interactions, and each value is relative to the system interacted with, much as velocity in classical mechanics is a property of one body relative to another. Wigner's friend stops being paradoxical: relative to the friend the result is definite, relative to Wigner the lab is in superposition, and the interference Wigner could observe is compatible with the friend's determinate observation. Rovelli also hoped to rebuild the quantum formalism from a few informational postulates, and his emphasis on information influenced the birth of QBism.

The price is a world built from perspectives. Emily Adlam argued in 2022 that views denying observer-independence challenge the intersubjective agreement about outcomes on which science depends, and Jacques Pienaar formulated five no-go theorems in 2021 suggesting that RQM's balance between relative values and absolute events cannot be sustained.4 Adlam and Rovelli responded in 2023 with a cross-perspective link postulate: measuring a system's pointer accurately reveals the outcome that system registered in an earlier interaction, unless the pointer has been tampered with.5 Whether this restores objectivity without smuggling back absolute facts is still argued.

title: Many Worlds
description: Everett's pure wave mechanics, branching through decoherence, and the fight over probability

concepts.title: Everett's Pure Wave Mechanics
concepts.contentHtml:
Hugh Everett III was a physics graduate student at Princeton when he proposed the boldest response to Bell's dilemma: take neither horn. Keep the wavefunction as the complete description, keep the Schrödinger equation exact, and simply drop the collapse dynamics. The result is pure wave mechanics. In January 1956 he gave his adviser, John Wheeler, a long draft thesis titled "Wave Mechanics Without Probability".1 Wheeler insisted on revisions, partly because Niels Bohr disapproved of Everett's critical approach, and the much shorter thesis was accepted in March 1957, with a paper on the same material published that July.2 Everett had already taken a job outside academia as a defence analyst in the spring of 1956.3

His key idea was the relative state. After a measurement, the universal wavefunction contains one term in which the system is "up" and the observer remembers "up", and another in which both say "down". Neither term is privileged; each copy of the observer has a perfectly consistent memory, and relative to each there is a definite outcome. Everett was explicit: "All elements of a superposition must be regarded as simultaneously existing". He also held, unlike later many-worlds theorists, that other branches remain in principle detectable.4

The physicist Bryce DeWitt at first objected that the theory's surplus structure made it too rich to represent the world we experience. In a letter of 7 May 1957 to Wheeler he granted that the scheme was "beautifully consistent"; but, as he put it, the memory of a real observer "does not branch". DeWitt came round, and his 1970 Physics Today article publicised the splitting-worlds picture5 now called the many-worlds interpretation. Keep the distinction in mind: Jeffrey Barrett, for one, reserves the name for DeWitt's splitting-worlds view and treats Everett's own relative-state theory as a separate thing to interpret.

concepts.title: Branches from Decoherence
concepts.contentHtml:
For decades many worlds faced a technical objection, the preferred basis problem. The mathematics allows infinitely many ways to decompose the quantum state of the universe into a superposition of orthogonal states.1 Write a cat's state in the dead-or-alive basis and you get two familiar worlds; write it in another basis and you get two bizarre ones. Which decomposition marks out the worlds? Adding a preferred basis by hand looked like exactly the sort of extra postulate Everett had wanted to avoid.

Decoherence transformed the debate. Environments constantly monitor macroscopic objects in roughly the position basis, and the resulting branches are dynamically robust: once a branch has spread records of itself into countless photons and air molecules, it evolves as if the others were not there. Saunders and Wallace argued that worlds are not fundamental at all. They are emergent structures in the universal wavefunction, defined well enough for all practical purposes though not with perfect precision, a view David Wallace set out at length in his 2012 book The Emergent Multiverse. On Wallace's picture, branching is local: worlds spread with the velocity of light and do not describe the whole of space at once.2

The standing objection is Ockham's razor. Much of the opposition to many worlds comes from its vast number of unobservable worlds, an apparently extreme violation of the principle that entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity. Everettians reply that the razor also counts laws: physical laws should not be multiplied beyond necessity either,3 and many worlds has the leanest dynamics of any realist option, with no extra variables and no collapse law. Hemmo and Shenker grant that the postulates are economical but argue that the advantage is irrelevant,4 since the postulates alone are not enough to explain our experience.

concepts.title: The Probability Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Many worlds meets its hardest test over probability. Standard quantum mechanics says a measurement yields "up" with probability 0.9 and "down" with 0.1. In Everett's theory both outcomes certainly occur. What can "90 per cent" mean when everything happens, and why should the squared amplitude, rather than a simple count of branches, guide your expectations? Three main strategies have been tried:

  • Decision theory. In 1999 David Deutsch argued that a special probabilistic axiom is unnecessary: all the practical consequences follow from the non-probabilistic axioms of quantum theory together with the non-probabilistic part of classical decision theory.1 A rational agent who knows she will branch should weight her bets by the Born rule. Wallace developed the argument further in 2007.
  • Self-locating uncertainty. Following Lev Vaidman, Charles Sebens and Sean Carroll note that between decoherence splitting the branches and your registering the result, you do not know which branch you are in. They argue that the Born rule is the uniquely rational way to apportion that credence, relying on one principle: changes purely to the environment do not affect the probabilities you should assign to outcomes in a local subsystem.2
  • Measure of existence. Vaidman treats the squared amplitude as a measure of how much each world exists, and cares about worlds in proportion to it.

None of these has won general assent. Recent derivations by decision theory and by symmetry arguments have faced strong opposition,3 and whether self-location can resolve the problem is highly controversial.4 A vivid test case is quantum Russian roulette: someone who would never play the classical game might seem rational to play endlessly if a quantum measurement controls the trigger, since some copy always survives. Vaidman's answer is no, because the worlds in which he is dead have a much larger measure of existence than those in which he is alive and rich.5 Defenders add a modest point: other interpretations simply postulate the Born rule, so many worlds is at no disadvantage here, even if it has no advantage either.

title: Pilot Waves and Collapse
description: Bohmian trajectories and GRW spontaneous collapse: two ways to add to quantum theory, and their tests

concepts.title: Bohmian Mechanics: The Impossible Done
concepts.contentHtml:
In Bohmian mechanics, also called the de Broglie-Bohm theory or the pilot-wave theory, the answer to "where is the electron?" is always: somewhere definite. Particles have positions at all times, and the wavefunction does not describe them; it guides them. The theory is defined by two equations: the ordinary Schrödinger equation for the wavefunction, and a first-order guiding equation that gives each particle's velocity in terms of the wavefunction. Fix the initial positions and the configuration evolves by a deterministic motion choreographed by the wavefunction.

Louis de Broglie found an equation of particle motion equivalent to the guiding equation in 1927, and explained at that year's Solvay Congress how it could account for interference.1 David Bohm rediscovered the theory in 1952,2 showing explicitly how extra parameters could turn the indeterministic description into a deterministic one. The timing mattered. John von Neumann had claimed to prove that a deterministic completion of quantum theory was mathematically impossible, and many physicists treated the matter as closed. Bell later wrote: "But in 1952 I saw the impossible done.3" He judged von Neumann's assumptions so unreasonable that "the proof of von Neumann is not merely false but foolish!4"

How does a deterministic theory reproduce quantum randomness? Through the quantum equilibrium hypothesis: if particle positions are distributed according to \(|\psi|^2\), the theory's predictions agree with standard quantum mechanics, including the Born rule and the appearance of collapse. Randomness is ignorance of exact initial positions, as in classical statistical mechanics, and no special measurement law is needed: an outcome is simply where particles, such as those of a pointer, end up. The theory accounts for all the phenomena of nonrelativistic quantum mechanics, from interference effects to spectral lines to spin.5

The wavefunction lives on configuration space, though, so one particle's velocity can depend instantly on the positions of distant ones. Bohmian mechanics is explicitly nonlocal, and Bell showed that any hidden-variable formulation of quantum mechanics must be.6

concepts.title: GRW: Collapse as a Law of Nature
concepts.contentHtml:
The other horn of Bell's dilemma says the Schrödinger equation is not quite right. In 1986 Ghirardi, Rimini and Weber produced the first satisfactory explicit model of how it might fail.1 Their theory, GRW, at first called Quantum Mechanics with Spontaneous Localisations, adds one random process to the dynamics. Each elementary constituent of matter suffers, at random times, a spontaneous localisation or "hit":2 its wavefunction is multiplied by a narrow Gaussian centred on some point, chosen most often where standard quantum mechanics says the particle is most likely to be found. The new dynamics is nonlinear and stochastic, and collapse no longer waits for an observer; it is something matter simply does.

Everything depends on two constants. GRW chose a hit rate of \(f = 10^{-16}\) per second and a localisation width of \(d = 10^{-5}\) cm. A microscopic system is therefore localised on average once every hundred million years,3 so atoms and molecules behave as ordinary quantum mechanics predicts. But a pointer contains an enormous number of particles, and in a superposition of two pointer positions every one of them sits in a different place in the two terms. A hit on any one of them suppresses a whole term. The effective rate is amplified by the number of particles, so a macroscopic object is localised about every \(10^{-7}\) seconds. As Bell put it, the cat "is not both dead and alive for more than a split second4".

Collapse theories have puzzles of their own. Gaussian hits leave tails: the collapsed wavefunction is tiny but not zero far away, so in what sense is the pointer really here? Such worries sharpened the demand that a theory state its primitive ontology, what it is fundamentally about. GRW can be read as a theory of a mass density spread through space, or, following a suggestion of Bell's, of flashes, the space-time points at which hits occur. With flashes as its ontology, Tumulka built a relativistic version of GRW in 2006 for non-interacting distinguishable particles.5

concepts.title: Paying the Price: Relativity, Worlds and Experiments
concepts.contentHtml:
Both programmes buy definite outcomes, and much of the bill is paid to relativity. Bohmian mechanics requires a distinguished relation of distant simultaneity,1 a preferred way of slicing spacetime into instants. Collapse theories can avoid a preferred slicing, as Tumulka's flash model shows, but only by deviating from quantum mechanics. Tumulka summed up the choice the present models offer: "either the conventional understanding of relativity is not right, or quantum mechanics is not exact2".

Bohm also faces a charge from the Everettian side. In 1996 David Deutsch argued that the empty branches of the pilot wave obey the same laws as the occupied one, so they are worlds too: "pilot-wave theories are parallel-universes theories in a state of chronic denial.3" Bohmians reply that branches of the wavefunction are not worlds unless something occupies them. Which side you find compelling depends partly on whether you accept a functionalist view, on which suitable patterns in the wavefunction count as worlds simply by having the right structure.

Here collapse theories have an advantage: they are testable. By modifying the dynamics they predict tiny deviations from standard quantum mechanics, and experiments now hunt for them with nanomechanical cantilevers cooled to millikelvin temperatures, levitated particles and the gravitational-wave detectors LIGO, AURIGA and LISA Pathfinder.4 One target is the Diósi-Penrose model, in which Roger Penrose proposed that a superposition collapses as a back-reaction from spacetime, curved differently by each branch. Its randomness makes particles diffuse, and diffusing charged particles radiate. Sandro Donadi, Angelo Bassi and colleagues looked for that faint radiation in a dedicated experiment at the Gran Sasso underground laboratory, and their result rules out the natural parameter-free version of the model.5 Collapse models with adjustable parameters survive, but experiments keep narrowing the room they have.

title: The Arrow of Time
description: Why time-symmetric laws give a one-way world: Boltzmann, the Past Hypothesis, and its critics

concepts.title: Reversible Laws, Irreversible World
concepts.contentHtml:
Film two billiard balls colliding and run it backwards: nothing looks wrong. Run a film of an egg breaking backwards and everyone laughs. The laws of classical mechanics are time-reversal invariant: for every solution, reversing all velocities and replacing \(t\) by \(-t\) gives another solution. Yet the large-scale world is full of one-way processes, summed up by the second law of thermodynamics. Where does the asymmetry come from?

Ludwig Boltzmann thought he had derived it. His 1872 paper, usually abbreviated Weitere Studien, contained the Boltzmann equation and the H-theorem,1 which seemed to prove that a gas must approach equilibrium. In 1876 Johann Loschmidt raised the reversibility objection: reverse every molecular velocity in a gas that has spread out, and the same laws carry it back to its unlikely starting state, so no theorem derived from time-symmetric mechanics alone can deliver one-way behaviour. Ernst Zermelo added the recurrence objection in 1896: a bounded system left to itself eventually returns arbitrarily close to its initial state.2

Boltzmann's response, in 1877, was a very different, combinatorial analysis.3 Equilibrium corresponds to overwhelmingly more microscopic arrangements than order does, so entropy increase is not certain, merely overwhelmingly probable. But that answer has a sting. The counting is itself time-symmetric, so applied to the past it says the gas was probably more disordered an hour ago too. Statistics alone predicts entropy rising in both directions away from now, contradicting your memories and every record you have.

Could the laws be asymmetric after all? Weak interactions between quarks and leptons do violate time-reversal symmetry, and in 2012 the BaBar collaboration, using 468 million pairs of B mesons produced at SLAC, reported a direct observation of the effect. Yet these violations do not appear to be responsible for thermodynamic behaviour,4 so the puzzle remains.

concepts.title: The Past Hypothesis
concepts.contentHtml:
The standard answer puts the asymmetry not in the laws but in a boundary condition. If the universe began in a state of extraordinarily low entropy, an extremely tiny section of its available phase space, then entropy has been climbing ever since, and statistical reasoning works towards the future because the past is pinned in place. Boltzmann saw that such a hypothesis was necessary, and so did Einstein, Richard Feynman and Erwin Schrödinger.1 The philosopher David Albert, in his 2000 book Time and Chance, gave it the name now standard:2 the Past Hypothesis.

Boltzmann himself preferred a different story: the observable universe might be a natural statistical fluctuation away from equilibrium within a vastly larger universe.3 The trouble is that small fluctuations are far more probable than large ones, so on this story it seems likelier that your memories of the past are themselves a fluke than that the past really happened as you remember it. The Past Hypothesis avoids this by making the low-entropy beginning a posit rather than a fluctuation.

It raises its own questions. Roger Penrose estimated that, judged by the standard measure on phase space, the probability of the universe starting in such a state is astronomically small.4 One reply is that the Past Hypothesis is a law, in which case its probability is simply one. Another question is whether it needs explaining at all: Craig Callender is sceptical that it does, while Huw Price takes the opposite position. Note too that classical mechanics is equally compatible with a "Future Hypothesis" of very low entropy in the distant future.5 The asymmetry of our world comes from an asymmetry in its boundary conditions, and nobody yet knows why the boundary conditions are asymmetric.

concepts.title: Critics, Cosmology and the Other Arrows
concepts.contentHtml:
The sharpest critic is John Earman, who concluded in 2006 that the Past Hypothesis is not even coherent enough to be false.1 His main complaint is that nobody can state it in the language of general relativity.2 Entropy for self-gravitating systems is slippery: for a gas in a box, spreading out raises entropy, but gravity makes matter clump, so a smooth early universe counts as low entropy. Loosely associating gravitational homogeneity with low entropy, cosmic inflation is arguably a source of a low-entropy initial condition, though in cosmology the line between laws and boundary conditions is especially slippery, so it is often unclear what such proposals really explain.

Some physicists try to do without a special beginning. In 2004 Sean Carroll and Jennifer Chen suggested that spontaneous eternal inflation could explain the arrow. Starting from empty de Sitter space, inflation can increase the total entropy of the universe without bound, creating universes like ours along the way. A striking consequence is that inflation occurs both forwards and backwards in time, so the universe is statistically time-symmetric on ultra-large scales3 and our arrow is a local feature.

The thermodynamic arrow is not the only one, and philosophers ask how the others relate to it:

  • Radiation: waves spread outward from concentrated charges, much as a released gas spreads into an expanding sphere. In a 1909 debate Einstein and Walther Ritz apparently disagreed about which asymmetry explains which.4
  • Knowledge: a footprint on a beach lets you infer that someone walked by earlier, rather than that the ordered mark arose as a random fluctuation. Grünbaum and Smart developed entropic accounts of this asymmetry.
  • Psychology: you remember the past, not the future. Suhler and Callender ground this arrow on the causal and knowledge asymmetries.5

Whether all of these flow from the Past Hypothesis plus statistical mechanics remains an open question.

title: Spacetime: Substance, Relations and Beyond
description: Newton versus Leibniz, Einstein's hole argument, and how quantum gravity may dissolve space and time

concepts.title: Newton's Bucket and Leibniz's Objection
concepts.contentHtml:
Is space a thing in its own right, a container that would exist even if emptied of matter, or only a system of relations between material things? The first view is substantivalism, the second relationalism, and the classic battle was fought between Isaac Newton and Leibniz. Newton's 1687 Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy relied on absolute space; Leibniz attacked it in his correspondence with Samuel Clarke in 1715–1716.1 Newton's own view was subtle. Absolute space was not material, and not quite a substance, since it lacks causal powers, but it would exist even in a vacuum, so it was not a mere attribute of bodies either. He treated it as a kind of pseudo-substance.2

Leibniz's sharpest objection exploits Galilean relativity. Newton's laws make a closed system evolve identically whether or not it moves with some extra constant velocity, just as Galileo noted that an experimenter in a cabin cannot tell whether his ship is at rest in harbour or sailing smoothly. So absolute velocity, though well defined in Newton's theory, cannot in principle be determined by experiment.3 Leibniz argued that differences which are unobservable in principle are not genuine differences at all, and that absolute space, which would make them real, must be a fiction.

The Newtonian answer, which Clarke pressed against Leibniz, was that acceleration, unlike velocity, does show up. In Newton's famous bucket argument, compare a bucket of water just set spinning on a cord with the same bucket and water later rotating together. In the first case the surface is flat; in the second it is concave, as the water recedes from the axis. Newton also imagined two globes joined by a cord far from any other bodies:4 the tension in the cord would reveal their rotation with nothing to rotate relative to. Mach later objected that Newton's argument leaves open the possibility that true rotation is relative to something, perhaps the fixed stars.5 The debate settled into an asymmetry that physics inherited: velocity looks relative, but acceleration looks absolute.

concepts.title: Einstein's Hole Argument
concepts.contentHtml:
The sharpest modern argument about substantivalism came from Einstein, in the middle of his struggle for general relativity. In mid-1913 he published a compromise theory that was not generally covariant,1 because he could not see how generally covariant equations could reduce to Newton's theory for weak fields. Later in 1913 he tried to turn that failure into a victory of sorts, arguing that no generally covariant theory at all is admissible,2 since any such theory would violate what he called the Law of Causality, which we would now call determinism. His tool was the hole argument.

Here is the modern form. Take a solution of the field equations and a region of spacetime, the hole. Because the theory is generally covariant, you can smoothly redistribute the metric field inside the hole while leaving everything outside untouched, and the result is still a solution. If spacetime points are real things, as the substantivalist says, the two solutions describe different physical situations, since a given point inside the hole has different metrical properties in each. But they agree everywhere outside, including the entire past. So the state of the world outside the hole fails to fix what happens inside: substantivalism appears to make general relativity indeterministic, about differences no observation could ever detect.

Einstein settled on generally covariant equations in November 1915, and defended them with the point-coincidence argument, which amounts to a defence of Leibniz Equivalence: solutions related by such a redistribution represent the same physical world. John Stachel brought the argument's significance to modern historians and philosophers in 1980,3 and in 1987 John Earman and John Norton recast it as a direct attack on spacetime substantivalism.4

Substantivalists have answers. Tim Maudlin's metric essentialism holds that each spacetime point carries its metrical properties essentially.5 Anti-haecceitist substantivalism denies that points have identities across possible worlds, so the two solutions are not two possibilities at all; this position is currently a popular response.6

concepts.title: Quantum Gravity: Does Spacetime Dissolve?
concepts.contentHtml:
General relativity is a classical theory, and joining it with quantum theory remains unsolved. One lesson many draw from the hole argument is background independence: no successful quantum theory of gravity can be set against an independent container spacetime. Loop quantum gravity theorists have used this as a criticism of string theory, which is formulated on a background spacetime.1

Background independence brings the problem of time. In canonical quantum gravity the super-Hamiltonian constraint, known as the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, does not generate change the way an ordinary Hamiltonian does: quantum states do not evolve under it, and there are no real instants for a state to describe. Julian Barbour concludes that time is illusory.2 Steven Weinstein argues instead that the constraint should not be expected to generate time evolution, and that one or more true Hamiltonians must play that role. Gryb and Thébault have argued that the hole argument and the problem of time are essentially the same problem.3

Several approaches suggest that spacetime itself is not fundamental. In loop quantum gravity the area and volume operators have discrete spectra, hinting at grainy space near the Planck length of about \(10^{-33}\) cm, although the result has been shown only for gauge-variant quantities.4 In string theory the AdS/CFT duality makes a ten-dimensional string theory observationally equivalent to a four-dimensional gauge theory without gravity,5 so neither description, and neither spacetime, looks fundamental. Mark Van Raamsdonk argued in 2010 that the connectedness of spacetime is tied to entanglement: disentangle the degrees of freedom of two regions and they pull apart and pinch off.6 Maldacena and Susskind's 2013 ER = EPR conjecture links entangled black holes to wormholes.

If spacetime is emergent, a new puzzle appears: how can a theory without fundamental space and time connect with observation, when arguably only entities localised in spacetime can ever be observed?7 Nick Huggett and Christian Wüthrich survey the theories and sketch how this can generally be answered. Newton's container and Leibniz's relations may both give way to a third option: spacetime as a pattern in something that is neither.
